open-question.question: The runner of Gurita for VS Code waits for a keypress after every chain and after every looped task run. A new setting is to close the terminal by itself when a chain ran all its lines. Does the setting also close the terminal of a looped task run that completed every task?
open-question.recommendation: The recorded default speaks of one setting a user turns off to keep every terminal open, and the runner ends a chain and a looped run the same way, so one rule serves both: the looped run is the long unattended one whose blocked page the setting exists to free, what it completed stays in its `Task-completion:` commits, which the page's completed-task list shows, and a stopped loop still waits.
open-question.alternative: The one new setting governs both kinds of run. With it on, a looped task run that ends on `Loop finished: no task remains` (the runner's `finished` outcome, reached once no `##` heading is left in `TASKS_TODO.md`) prints its report and exits without waiting for a keypress, so its terminal closes and the page unblocks. A loop that stopped (an unresolved assignment, a task that did not end on `Task completed.`, or an unreadable task list) still waits for a keypress, as a stopped chain does. One rule for every run: `run_chain` and `run_loop` already end the same way (report, `wait_for_key`, exit 0 when finished), so the setting skips the same wait at both, and the looped run, which is the long unattended run where an unblocked page on success matters most, gets the benefit too. The loop's closing report (`Tasks completed: N`) and every task session's output vanish with the terminal on success, leaving only the commits and the refreshed page as the record; the setting's description and the README must say it reaches looped runs, since the tracker entry names only chains.

The setting closes only a chain's terminal. A looped task run keeps waiting for a keypress after its report whatever the setting says and however the loop ended, exactly as today. Follows the tracker entry's wording literally and keeps the one run that can complete many tasks unattended always reviewable at its end, with the runner's loop path left unchanged. A loop that completed every task still leaves the mission's page blocked until someone presses a key, the very wait the setting exists to remove, and a user who turned the setting on is likely to read the loop's lingering terminal as the setting not working.

Looped runs get a setting of their own beside the chain one: with it on, a looped task run that ends on `Loop finished: no task remains` exits without waiting for a keypress, while a stopped loop still waits; the chain setting does not reach loops and the loop setting does not reach chains. Lets a user auto-close short chains while still reviewing the output of a long multi-task run, or the reverse, without either choice being forced on the other. Adds a second setting to the manifest, its description, and the README for a distinction few users are likely to want, and needs a default of its own, which depends on how the default of the chain setting is settled.

open-question.question: No recipe in `gurita-vscode/shipped_recipes.md`, the recipe file Gurita for VS Code ships, holds a `codex` line, and the file is to gain one. Which shipped recipes gain a Codex line: a single-task line, one variant of one chain, or a Codex variant of several chains?
open-question.applied-principle: Check tier claims against the live environment
open-question.recommendation: With the mixed-agent variant leaving, a named single-task recipe is how the shipped file carries Antigravity, and a Codex one beside it with `-m` gives Codex's model list, the line's own dropdown, and the switch's first model a shipped value, as every shipped `claude` and `agy` line does; the id is taken from the catalog `codex debug models` prints (on 0.159.3 `gpt-6-luna`, `gpt-5.6-terra`, and `gpt-5.6-luna`), and the Renamed chain lines decision, leaving the renamed chain one variant, closes both several-chains options.
open-question.alternative: The same single `Single task (Codex)` recipe, its one headless `codex exec '$gurita:complete-task …' --dangerously-bypass-approvals-and-sandbox` line also carrying `-m` with a named Codex model id. The recipe name says the model, as the Claude Code single-task names do. No chain or button recipe changes. As small as the account-default single-task line, and it also gives the Settings window's Codex model list a shipped entry. The shipped line then gets its own model dropdown, so Codex in the harness dropdown has a model to offer from the first run. It pins a model id that was not part of the 2026-11-22 check. That id can go stale or be unavailable on a given account, and the line then stops a run that would have worked at the account's default. Only task completion reaches Codex.

One new single-task recipe, `Single task (Codex)`, beside the three existing ones: one headless line `codex exec '$gurita:complete-task --mission <path> <Task Title>' --dangerously-bypass-approvals-and-sandbox`, in the form `docs/ways-of-using.md` gives, carrying no `-m`. No chain gains a variant and no button recipe changes. The smallest change that ships a Codex line. A `task_line_rules.txt` rule can send matching tasks of a looped run to Codex, the same way the Antigravity single-task line is used. The line is one task's run, in the headless form the 2026-11-22 check confirmed, and it runs on any Codex account because it names no model. A Codex user still has no chain to fire from a mission page, so every workflow step outside task completion stays Claude Code or Antigravity. With no `-m` on any shipped Codex line, the Settings window's Codex model list, which is read from `-m` on `codex` lines, gets nothing from the shipped file.

One chain gains one variant: `Execute tasks` gets a `Codex` variant holding one headless line, `codex exec '$gurita:complete-all-tasks --mission <path>' --dangerously-bypass-approvals-and-sandbox`, with no `-m`. Its two Claude Code variants stay interactive. No single-task recipe or other chain changes. A Codex user can fire it straight from the variant dropdown at the execute-tasks step. The chain is one skill, and the host suite has already seen it on Codex, dispatching complete-task agents through `spawn_agent` in rounds. A whole run can be handed to Codex without writing a rule file. The line is headless while its sibling variants are interactive, so the chain ends with no session left open. Its run, many agents under `agents.max_threads` rounds, is longer and less checked end to end than a single task. Codex reaches no step before execution, and no Codex line puts an entry in the Settings model list.

alternative.id: Mixed-agent variant with one Codex line

open-question.alternative: One chain gains one mixed-agent variant, on the pattern of the existing `Mixed-agent (Gemini reviews, Claude annotates)` variant. Exactly one of its lines is a headless `codex exec '$gurita:<skill> …' --dangerously-bypass-approvals-and-sandbox` line with no `-m`, for example the alternatives pass in a `First run` variant, and the chain's other lines stay `claude` lines. No single-task recipe changes. It fits a pattern the shipped file already teaches, one harness taking one pass of a chain. It puts Codex where an independent second model adds the most, without asking a user to trust Codex with a whole chain. Running the variant needs two harnesses installed and signed in, so it is not a Codex-only path. Which chain and which pass to choose is a judgment the file then stands behind. If the chosen chain is `Requirements iteration`, the variant depends on how the lines of that renamed chain end up.

Every chain whose steps all have a headless form gains a `Codex` variant made only of `codex exec '$gurita:<skill> …' --dangerously-bypass-approvals-and-sandbox` lines with no `-m`: `First run`, `Requirements iteration`, `Prepare tasks`, `Prepare and Execute tasks`, `Execute tasks`, and `Finish mission`. The chains that end on an interactive `claude` line get a headless Codex line there instead. A `Single task (Codex)` recipe of the same form stands beside them. Button recipes do not change. A Codex-only user can fire every workflow step from a mission page and send looped-run tasks to Codex. Codex then stands as a full third harness, matching the harness check and install support the extension already gives it. It adds the most to the shipped file: seven new variant blocks to keep in step with their Claude Code siblings. Only the single-line headless form has been checked, so whole chains, the review and recommendation passes among them, would ship unverified on Codex. The `Requirements iteration` variant depends on how the lines of that renamed chain end up. No line seeds the Settings model list.

alternative.id: Codex variants of several chains with model

open-question.alternative: The same full set: `Codex` variants of `First run`, `Requirements iteration`, `Prepare tasks`, `Prepare and Execute tasks`, `Execute tasks`, and `Finish mission`, plus a Codex single-task recipe. Every line is headless `codex exec '$gurita:<skill> …' --dangerously-bypass-approvals-and-sandbox` and carries `-m` with a named Codex model id, chosen per line as the Claude Code lines choose their families. Codex becomes a full third harness, and every shipped Codex line also has its own model dropdown. The Settings window's Codex model list starts filled from the shipped file, and the chains can give the heavy passes and the light ones different models, as the Claude Code chains do. The largest change and the most exposed to drift. Every line pins an id that no check has covered, so a model retired or missing on an account breaks every Codex chain at once. The `Requirements iteration` variant depends on how the lines of that renamed chain end up.

open-question.question: The recipe `Requirements iteration` that Gurita for VS Code ships is to be renamed "Approve all standing recommendations and review again". The old name also heads a recipe in `snippets/GURITA_USAGE.md`, the hand-use document no tool reads. Is that recipe renamed there too?
open-question.recommendation: One chain keeps one name across the repository for a one-line edit in a file no tool reads, and the lines under the heading equal the shipped `default` variant's, which the Renamed chain lines decision keeps unchanged; that decision also takes the mixed-agent variant out of the shipped file, which closes folding the snippet's mixed-agent recipe in to match it.
open-question.alternative: The `### Requirements iteration` heading in `snippets/GURITA_USAGE.md` is renamed to `### Approve all standing recommendations and review again` in this mission, in the same change that renames the shipped recipe. Only the heading changes: its `Stage: additional review round` line stays, the separate `### Mixed-agent requirements review (Gemini reviews, Claude annotates)` recipe beside it keeps its own name and form, and the file's other recipes are untouched. One chain carries one name across the repository. The listing README tells readers the snippet file holds "the same recipes" as the shipped file, so a reader moving between the button and the hand-use document finds the chain under the name the button shows. The edit is one line in a file no tool reads, so nothing can break. The edit reaches a root-level file outside the mission's `gurita-vscode/` scope, which is adjacent work, not core work. The snippet's mixed-agent chain stays a recipe of its own while the shipped file holds it as a variant of the renamed recipe, so the two documents still differ in shape. Whether the snippet's lines under the new heading still match its name depends on how the sibling question on the renamed chain's lines is settled.

The heading is renamed to `### Approve all standing recommendations and review again` as in the heading-only option, and the snippet's `### Mixed-agent requirements review (Gemini reviews, Claude annotates)` recipe moves under it as a second `####` variant, so the renamed recipe holds `#### default` and `#### Mixed-agent (Gemini reviews, Claude annotates)` as the shipped file does. The variant form is one the snippet file already describes in its `## Recipes` introduction and uses for `Execute tasks`. Every other recipe in the file stays as it is. The hand-use document then holds this chain in the same shape and under the same name as the shipped file, so the README's statement that it holds "the same recipes" is true for this chain, and a reader copying either variant by hand finds both under the one heading the button shows. It goes beyond renaming: it restructures a document no tool reads, outside the mission's scope and outside any tracker entry, and it removes a heading (`Mixed-agent requirements review …`) that hand users may know. The mixed-agent variant's lines differ from the default's in order and harness, so whether they still fit the new name depends on how the sibling question on the renamed chain's lines is settled.

`snippets/GURITA_USAGE.md` is not edited by this mission. Its `### Requirements iteration` recipe keeps its heading and lines, and only the shipped file, the extension's tests, the listing README, and the `CLAUDE.md` layout entry move to the new name. Any later rename is left to whoever next edits the hand-use document, and this mission plans none. The mission stays inside its `gurita-vscode/` scope and inside what the tracker asks for, which is a rename of the recipe Gurita for VS Code ships. The snippet file is read by no tool and the extension already does not mirror it (its mixed-agent chain is a separate recipe there and a variant in the shipped file), so leaving it changes no behaviour. The repository then names one chain two ways, and the listing README, which points readers to the snippet file as holding the same recipes, sends them to a document where the button's name does not appear. The mismatch persists with no task recording it, so it is likely to stay until someone notices.

open-question.question: In the Settings window of Gurita for VS Code, a recipe line's harness dropdown is to offer Codex beside Claude Code and Antigravity. A headless line has a documented Codex form, `codex exec '$gurita:<skill> …' --dangerously-bypass-approvals-and-sandbox`, and that form is the only one checked on Codex. An interactive line, a bare `claude "…"` or an `agy -i "…"` ending in `# interactive`, opens on the prompt and keeps its session open, and no Codex form is recorded for it. What does switching an interactive line to Codex give?
open-question.applied-principle: Check tier claims against the live environment
open-question.recommendation: It offers Codex on the lines the shipped recipes make interactive and keeps the conversational ones conversations, trusting the bare `codex` form only once it has been run, as the headless form was; the installed 0.159.3's help already gives `codex [OPTIONS] [PROMPT]` with `-m`, `-c`, and the bypass flag, and shows that `-i` there attaches an image, so an `agy` line's `-i` has to go.
open-question.alternative: The dropdown offers Codex on an interactive line, and the switch keeps the line interactive: the command word becomes a bare `codex` (no `exec`, the form `codex --help` gives as `codex [OPTIONS] [PROMPT]`), the prompt is rewritten from `"/gurita:…"` to `'$gurita:…'`, `--dangerously-skip-permissions` becomes `--dangerously-bypass-approvals-and-sandbox`, the model and effort are written as `-m` and `-c model_reasoning_effort=…` as the recorded Codex-effort decision sets, any `-i` an `agy` line carried is dropped, and the trailing `# interactive` mark is kept. Switching such a line back gives `claude "…"` or `agy -i "…"`, so the interactive form survives a round trip. Before the switch ships, the mission makes one hands-on check of that form on the installed `codex` (0.159.3 today): that a `$gurita:` skill named in the initial prompt runs and the session stays open on its result. The extension's documentation then gives the interactive Codex form beside the headless one as checked. The switch does what the user picked on every shipped interactive line, the conversational skills (`discuss-open-question`, `discuss-mission-goal`, `discuss-new-task`, the new `ask-in-mission-context` action) included, and the form it writes has been seen working rather than inferred, matching how the headless Codex form came to be trusted. It adds a hands-on check and a documentation entry to the mission, and if the check finds the TUI does not resolve `$gurita:` from an initial prompt, or stops on a trust or approval screen, the switch has no form to write and the question reopens. The single-quoted Codex prompt also means a value filled into it may hold no single quote, a quoting difference from the double-quoted `claude` and `agy` prompts.

The same rewrite as the checked form, a bare `codex '$gurita:…' --dangerously-bypass-approvals-and-sandbox` line with its `-m` and `-c model_reasoning_effort=…` values and its `# interactive` mark kept, reversible to `claude "…"` or `agy -i "…"`, but shipped on the strength of `codex --help`'s `[PROMPT]` argument ("Optional user prompt to start the session") and the interactive CLI accepting the same `-m`, `-c`, and bypass flags, with no hands-on check made in the mission. The documentation gives the form without claiming it was checked. The switch keeps every interactive line interactive at the lowest cost: no check to run and nothing that can stall the mission, the rewrite being a mechanical extension of `switchCommand` and the headless Codex rewrite. It ships a form the project has never run, against a requirement stance in which the only Codex form trusted is the checked headless one; if the TUI does not invoke the skill from the initial prompt, every switched interactive line silently opens a Codex session that never runs the skill, and the user learns it only in the terminal.

alternative.id: Headless codex exec for every line

open-question.alternative: Switching an interactive line to Codex writes the one checked Codex form, `codex exec '$gurita:…' --dangerously-bypass-approvals-and-sandbox` with its `-m` and `-c model_reasoning_effort=…` values, and drops the `# interactive` mark, so the line becomes headless and the runner treats it as one, reading its final message. No interactive Codex form is introduced. Switching it back gives a headless `claude -p "…"` or `agy -p "…"` line, since nothing records that it was interactive before. Every line the switch writes is in the only form checked on Codex, so nothing unverified ships, and a non-conversational interactive line such as `recommend-all-open-questions` or `complete-all-tasks` still runs to completion on Codex, its result now readable by the runner. The switch silently changes the line's kind: a conversational skill's line becomes a one-shot run with no follow-up, which defeats the reason those lines are interactive (the "Ask question input" decision keeps `ask-in-mission-context` open for follow-up questions), and the interactive form is lost on a switch back, so a Codex try-out cannot be undone through the dropdown alone.

alternative.id: Headless only where the skill is not conversational

open-question.alternative: Switching an interactive line to Codex reads the line's skill (`readSkill`) and acts by it: a line running a skill that finishes on its own (`recommend-all-open-questions`, `complete-all-tasks`, and the like) is rewritten to the checked headless `codex exec '$gurita:…'` form with its `# interactive` mark dropped, as in the headless option, while a line running a conversational skill (`discuss-open-question`, `discuss-mission-goal`, `discuss-new-task`, `ask-in-mission-context`) is refused with a message saying an interactive Codex form is not available, and the line stays as it is. A switch back from a converted line gives a headless `claude -p` or `agy -p` line. It uses only the checked Codex form and never turns a conversation into a one-shot run, while still letting the interactive lines whose skill needs no conversation move to Codex. The extension must hold a list of which skills are conversational, a piece of plugin knowledge kept in a second place that can drift as skills change, and the dropdown behaves differently for lines that look alike; converted lines still lose their interactive form on a switch back.

alternative.id: Codex not offered on interactive lines

open-question.alternative: The harness dropdown offers Codex on headless lines only: on an interactive line (one ending in `# interactive`, the runner's own test) it lists Claude Code and Antigravity, as `SWITCHABLE_HARNESSES` does today, and the line cannot be switched to Codex from the Settings window. A person who wants an interactive Codex line writes it by hand in a recipe file, where it keeps its harness as text, as a `codex` line does today; no interactive Codex form is documented or introduced, now or until a later mission records one. Nothing unchecked ships and no line ever changes kind behind the user's back; the change is the smallest, the dropdown's offer simply depending on the line's form, and it leaves the door open for a later mission to add the interactive form once one is checked. The new Codex choice is missing exactly on the lines the shipped recipes make interactive (the recommendation pass, every `complete-all-tasks` line, every discussion line), so a user moving a recipe to Codex must hand-edit those lines, and the dropdown's offer varying by line form needs a word of explanation in the Settings window or the README.

open-question.question: In the Settings window of Gurita for VS Code, a line switched to another harness takes that harness's first listed model and keeps its effort or takes the harness's first listed one, and today the switch is refused with an error when that harness's model list or effort list is empty. The harness dropdown is to offer Codex, whose model list and new effort list hold only the values that recipe lines and the person's own additions carry, so either list can be empty, while a Codex line can also run at the account's defaults with no model and no effort written. What happens when a line is switched to Codex while Codex's model list or effort list is empty?

recommendation.option: Require a model, omit an empty effort

open-question.recommendation: An empty effort list, the state of a fresh install, no longer blocks the switch, while every line the switch writes carries `-m` and so keeps its model and harness dropdowns and its way back, under the unchanged rule that a pick inserts no text; a model list emptied by hand still gets today's refusal, which says why.

alternative.id: Require a model, omit an empty effort

open-question.alternative: The two lists are treated differently: an empty model list still refuses the switch with today's error notification, while an empty effort list lets the switch go ahead with no effort override written, so the line runs at the account's default effort. A non-empty effort list gives the kept or first effort as decided. Picks still insert no text, so a Codex line written without the override has no effort dropdown until the flag is written by hand. Every Codex line the switch writes carries `-m`, which is what gives a Codex line its controls today, so the line keeps its model dropdown and its harness dropdown, while the new effort list, the one most likely to be empty, no longer blocks the switch. The rule is asymmetric and has to be explained, a switch is still blocked while the model list is empty, and a line written without the effort override cannot have its effort picked from the window later without a hand edit.

The switch to Codex keeps today's behaviour for an empty list: `rewriteHarness` refuses an offer listing no model or no effort, the Settings window tells it in its existing error notification (`The harness could not be changed: …`), and the line is left as it stands. The Codex option stays offered in the dropdown whatever its lists hold, and the person adds a model or an effort under Models and efforts before switching again. Nothing new is written for a Codex line with no model or no effort. No new code path: the existing refusal in `rewriteHarness` and `editLineHarness` already covers Codex once it is switchable, every Codex line the switch writes carries `-m` and the effort override and so always gets its model and effort dropdowns, and a switch back to Claude Code or Antigravity always has values to map. The dropdown offers a choice that fails only after it is picked, and while Codex's lists are empty (likely for the new effort list, filled only by Codex lines carrying the override) the switch is unusable until the person types entries by hand; whether the lists are empty in practice depends on what the shipped Codex line carries.

alternative.id: Disable Codex while a list is empty

open-question.alternative: The line's harness dropdown shows Codex as a disabled entry while Codex's model list or effort list is empty, its hover text naming the empty list and pointing at Models and efforts, so no switch to Codex reaches the host; once both lists hold an entry Codex is picked normally and takes the first model and the kept or first effort as decided. The host keeps `rewriteHarness`'s refusal as a guard behind it. Nothing is written for a Codex line with no model or no effort. The person learns why Codex cannot be picked before trying, with no error after a click, and every Codex line the switch writes still carries both values and so keeps both dropdowns and a switch back. The Settings page script must receive and track Codex's list state per line's dropdown and redraw it as the lists change, and the switch is still blocked whenever a list is empty, so a person content with the account's defaults must first invent an entry they do not want.

alternative.id: Omit the flag of an empty list

open-question.alternative: The switch always succeeds: for each of the two lists, a non-empty list gives its value as decided (the first model as `-m`, the kept or first effort as `-c model_reasoning_effort=<level>`), and an empty list gives no flag at all, so the line runs at the account's default model, default effort, or both. The rule that a model or effort pick inserts no text into a line stays, so a Codex line left without `-m` gets no model dropdown and one left without the override no effort dropdown until the flag is written by hand, and the existing refusal is removed for the Codex switch. Codex can be picked at once whatever its lists hold, and the line it writes is the account-defaults form a Codex line can legitimately take, with no invented value standing in it. A line written without a flag loses that value's control in the Settings window, and since today's line editor gives a Codex line controls only when it carries `-m`, a line written with no model shows as read-only text with no harness dropdown, so it cannot be switched back or given a model from the window even after the lists gain entries.

The switch always succeeds and writes no flag for an empty list, as in omitting the flag, and in addition a Codex line gets its harness, model, and effort controls whether or not it carries `-m` or the effort override: each dropdown opens on an "account default" entry standing for no flag, picking a listed value inserts `-m <model>` or `-c model_reasoning_effort=<level>` into the line's first command, and picking the default entry removes the flag. The module rule that a pick inserts no text is lifted for Codex lines, and a Codex line with no model or no effort can be switched back to Claude Code or Antigravity, taking that harness's first model and kept or first effort. Every Codex line, the account-defaults form included, stays fully editable from the Settings window, so an empty list never blocks the switch and never strands a line the switch wrote. The largest change: `lineValues.ts` gains flag insertion and removal, `lineEditor` and the page script gain a default entry and controls for flag-less lines, and the stored `custom N` variants and tests grow with them, all for a case that arises only while a list is empty.

When a list Codex's switch needs is empty, the host asks for the value in VS Code's own input box, the way the Settings window already asks for a list entry (one box per empty list, its validation refusing an empty entry), adds the typed value to Codex's list as the person's addition (`addedModels` or `addedEfforts`), and writes it into the line as decided; dismissing the box writes nothing, neither the line nor the list. A non-empty list is used without asking. The switch completes in one gesture with a real value the person chose, every Codex line written carries both flags and so keeps its dropdowns and a switch back, and the list is filled for every later switch. A dropdown pick opens a modal prompt the other switches never show, and the person must know a valid Codex model name or effort level to type, with no way through this path to say they want the account's default instead.

The extension ships a fixed default Codex model list and effort list (the effort list Codex's documented reasoning levels) laid beneath the values derived from recipe lines, so Codex's lists are never empty unless the person removes every entry through the existing `removedModels`/`removedEfforts` overlay; the switch takes the first listed model and the kept or first effort as decided, and a list the person has emptied refuses as today. The switch works out of the box on a fresh install with no shipped or own Codex line, and every line it writes carries both values and keeps its controls. It reverses the recorded rule that the extension ships no list of its own and queries no harness, and a built-in model name goes stale as Codex's models change, needing a release to update while a stale first entry is what every switch writes; how much it adds depends on what the shipped Codex line carries.
